source_facts.paraphrase: First distinguish palatal y from nonpalatal g. Nonpalatal g is a stopped g word-initially, after n and in gemination; elsewhere it is the continuous voiced back sound. Palatal g is y except after n, where the selected palatal outcome is the end of singe. This is more usable than three unexplained g sounds in a table.
source_facts.limits: The visible following vowel does not independently establish palatal status. Fulk names gǣstan as hard despite its front vowel; historical conditioning and word-specific evidence matter.

source_facts.paraphrase: Initial palatal g developed immediately before a front vowel or front diphthong. Medial/final g was palatalized after a front vowel unless immediately followed by a back vowel. Later mutation can conceal the original environment; Fulk also notes medial outcomes after mutated vowels.
source_facts.limits: These are historical conditions, not a claim that every present-day written e/æ/y makes g soft. The beginner should use a practical default plus a pronunciation note, not reconstruct a lost ending.

source_facts.paraphrase: Initial c was affricated in the initial front-vowel environments. Medially/finally, c differs from g: its conditions involved an earlier i-vowel or a following i/j, not any front vowel. A following back vowel could block the change; a following consonant could reverse it. Fulk gives dīċ/dīcas and miċel/micles, with analogy and other histories explicitly limiting mechanical inference.
source_facts.limits: Do not give g’s after-any-front-vowel rule to c. Do not give a blanket current-spelling rule c before a/o/u = k: sēcan and other old-j forms can still have ch. A few carefully selected form pairs clarify that an ending may change the sound without requiring a historical grammar lesson.

source_facts.paraphrase: Cook’s compact conditioning list places y/ȳ with guttural environments; Fulk distinguishes inherited/fronted vowels from later mutation and explicitly supplies contrary examples. The current guide groups e/i/æ/y without a usable decision and is particularly liable to cause false palatal readings beside y.
source_facts.limits: y/ȳ are front in tongue position, but that is not a reliable c/g prediction. Preserve cyrice’s explicitly supplied ch values; do not silently turn cynn/cyning or all mutated forms soft. No broad new y-rule is proposed.

source_facts.paraphrase: Read sc/cg/gg/ng as combinations before applying rules to an individual c or g. Initial sc normally has sh; ordinary cg/gg has the final sound of bridge, with hard-stop and compound-boundary exceptions. Ordinary ng has audible g as in finger, but selected palatal ng has the end of singe. Fulk’s sc discussion also gives real inflectional alternations.
source_facts.limits: Keep docga/frosc as already supplied worked exceptions, if retained. A complete predictive account of ng and medial sc is unnecessary at this stage; exceptional assessed forms need a pronunciation card. Do not claim ng is invariably finger or sc invariably sh.

source_facts.paraphrase: Keep the already contracted practical vowel and diphthong convention, audible unstressed vowels and macrons. Replace recycled exercises with new quantities and all six diphthong spellings; use Fulk’s selected diphthong values even when the form is taken from Cook.
source_facts.limits: Do not silently substitute Cook’s different diphthong sound table for the current Fulk-based convention. English glosses and course spelling stay explicit.

source_facts.paraphrase: Keep Fulk’s between-voiced-sounds f/s/th rule and its word-edge, voiceless-neighbour and lexical limits. New exercises must include voiced neighbours other than vowels and a voiceless consonant cluster, not just another between-two-vowels item.
source_facts.limits: The rule applies to the selected sound within its word; do not infer Old English voicing from its modern descendant or silently adopt Cook’s broader word-final voicing.

source_facts.paraphrase: Transfer the existing front/back h instructions, pronounced clusters, medial doubling and root-stress rules to new words. Final double spelling is not a demand for extra duration. ge- is unstressed; a prefixed verb normally stresses its root.
source_facts.limits: No new trill, aspiration system, phonetic-transcription exercise, or historical sound-change prerequisite is needed.

decision_procedure.name: Check a combination or lexical note first
decision_procedure.instruction: Identify sc, cg/gg and ng before treating c or g singly. Any explicitly supplied pronunciation for a word/form takes precedence. For a compound or prefix boundary, use the given division; do not invent a boundary from the letters.
decision_procedure.assessment: Regular combinations can be applied to unseen vetted words; an exception is supplied knowledge, never disguised as spelling deduction.

decision_procedure.name: Initial c
decision_procedure.instruction: Before a consonant or a/ā, o/ō, u/ū, the ordinary target is k (kit). Before e/ē, i/ī, æ/ǣ and the front diphthong spellings, ch (chin) is a useful default, with stated exceptions such as cēlan. Treat y/ȳ as needing the word’s pronunciation information, not as an automatic ch trigger.
decision_procedure.assessment: Use cuman/cnīf and cyrice/cēlan as retained worked support; reserve cēosað and other chosen pool words for transfer. Label the front-vowel branch a default, not an exceptionless law.

decision_procedure.name: C elsewhere
decision_procedure.instruction: Final c after i/ī, and c after i/ī before a non-back vowel, commonly has ch. A following consonant commonly requires k; dīc/dīcas and micel/micles show useful changes of form. Other positions, especially beside e/æ/y or in old-j verbs such as sēcan, need lexical guidance rather than a universal front-vowel rule.
decision_procedure.assessment: Test selected regular micel/micles or dīc/dīcas only after teaching the relevant positions. Do not require a beginner to identify an invisible old j. Do not generalize “any c next to a front vowel is ch.”

decision_procedure.name: Identify the y branch of g
decision_procedure.instruction: Initial g immediately before a front vowel/diphthong is often y (yes); g after a front vowel is often y when no back vowel follows. ge- is a particularly useful supplied y-prefix. Keep explicit hard-g exceptions beside later front vowels. The next printed vowel alone cannot always decide.
decision_procedure.assessment: Fresh regular gīet, fæger and regn support different positions. A note must identify an ambiguous exception such as gǣstan if used.

decision_procedure.name: Place nonpalatal g
decision_procedure.instruction: Once the word/form is known to be nonpalatal: use stopped g (go) at the beginning, after n or in a hard geminate; use continuous voiced back g elsewhere. The latter keeps the throat vibrating while the back of the tongue leaves a narrow gap near the g position. It can be held; stopped g cannot.
decision_procedure.assessment: Contrast fresh gān/gold/glæd with āgan; initial clusters matter, so the æ of glæd does not override the intervening l. This second step is a distribution rule, not a third unrelated sound to memorize.

decision_procedure.name: Use a bounded fallback honestly
decision_procedure.instruction: For a word whose spelling does not select a branch, consult the supplied sound note or dictionary evidence. A new exercise should either obey the taught default or give the needed lexical fact. A learner may correctly identify that spelling alone is insufficient.
decision_procedure.assessment: At most one or two explicit exception/application items; most tasks should ask a rule-based decision plus its relevant immediate context, followed by oral reading.

keep: All numbered Cook exercises and prompts; no omission or rewording
Current spelling, full paradigms and course teaching sequence
Selected Fulk-based vowel/diphthong/voicing convention and minimal IPA
change: Replace the c/g inventory-of-sounds paragraph with a short ordered procedure and position table
Distinguish single c/g from sc/cg/gg/ng before giving defaults
Teach initial versus medial/final positions and the stopped/continuous nonpalatal-g distribution
Make current-spelling limits explicit, especially y/ȳ and inflected forms
Replace original pronunciation practice with fresh word-forms and new phonological contexts across all skill groups
Keep assessed regular features unsolved in support; supply meaning, unrelated difficult features and genuine lexical exceptions only
do_not_expand: No complete historical reconstruction or new historical-grammar prerequisite
No silent addition of overpoints to the book or respelling of Cook
No IPA transcription drills or repeated full-word IPA
No change to Cook assignments or active grammatical production milestones

exercise_design.partition: Coordinator must reserve final assessment words before prose. None of the selected fresh task forms may be promoted into a worked example during drafting; source examples are evidence, not automatic teaching examples.
exercise_design.regularity: The fresh-word list is vetted to fit each stated branch. For arbitrary unknown words, the procedure includes an honest lexical fallback; it never claims that present-day spelling recovers every lost trigger.

tasks.aim: Notice quantity and apply the vowel values
tasks.proposal: Three new pairs for/fōr, węnde/wēnde, optionally tol/tōl; add dǣd/wīd or the rounded-y contrast as needed. Do not merely identify a macron: read the sound and distinguish duration from stress.

Mix initial, medial, final and before-consonant cases; ask the sound plus the immediate context that selects the taught branch. Use cēosað, micel/micles, gān, glæd, āgan, and either gīet/fæger/regn or reserve those for another group.

tasks.aim: Read combinations and absent English sounds
tasks.proposal: scūfan, brycg, singan, cwæð, riht/dohtor, hȳdan; no repeated cuman/scip/niht/wyrt items. Keep sc as a unit even before ū.

Cover all ea/ēa/eo/ēo/ie/īe with eall/scēap/heorte/frēond/scield/gīet, then ǣfre/fīf/cēosað/hæfð, sittan/sunne, gewrit/forlǣtan. Select a manageable subset; this is a pool, not an instruction to assess all 44 forms.

tasks.aim: Read a genuinely fresh short context
tasks.proposal: Reserve content words for a short new composition or an unchanged new source clause, give the complete English meaning, and ask for rule explanations without printing those very sound answers in the support table. Candidate compositions below are editorial proposals only.

exercise_design.exception_items: If desired, use gǣstan, mengan or mānful with the exceptional pronunciation explicitly supplied. Ask how the note overrides the default in the new context; do not grade an impossible spelling-only deduction.
exercise_design.grading: Accept the selected practical English cues or accurate tongue/airflow descriptions. Grade the sound decision and relevant condition; do not demand historical derivations, terminology not taught, translation or case recognition.
